POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
3. Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page
4. An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence of checks already made
5. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it
6. Understating is more insidious than overstating; a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions undermines good work
7. Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
8. Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
9. Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
12. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team
13. An open question has a cost; when the evidence leans one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on
14. Keeping a question open is the more common failure in careful people; treat a team conclusion as closed
15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
18. Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure
19. Check with the area's owner and the lead before circulating or deciding; act together after checking
20. When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one; trust experienced colleagues, shared records and agreed direction

RESPONSE:
Recalling from memory, so some wording will be approximate.

**Opening**
- Notes for new team members on working with the material and with people.
- It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It's written down because that practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight. Part comes from the evidence and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it.
- Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim and how closely. Colleagues with years in an area have tested things in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, since it reflects checks they've already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work done well.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports that its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position, and if a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Before responding, show you've taken in the message: restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. This isn't politeness; it keeps the conversation moving rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with. Find what's right, say so, and extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement make people defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step that shared understanding makes available.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the overall direction, pick up the points you can act on now, and say the budget will follow in due course.

**§3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material every time. A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or when asked.
- Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- The value of a shared record is building on it together. A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into private versions of the truth and stops being able to act.
- Example: the notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4. Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions the evidence settles and some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block dependent decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited if something new comes up; a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping a question open because one more check feels safer, is the more common one in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- Once the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

**§5. Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from elsewhere in the organisation see things differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful. A reviewer starting from scratch mostly rediscovers what the team already knows.
- So brief reviewers: what you've concluded, where you think the risks are, and what you'd like them to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- When you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time, so take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6. Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before taking a step you can see is good, check that it fits what the area's owners have in mind. Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release the result when it's ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and costs more than a short conversation first.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps don't need sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first and then act together.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether and how they'd like it restructured.

**§7. Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other.
- Overclaiming / second-guessing
- Inventing a flaw / overlooking one
- Closing too early / keeping open too long
- Abandoning a line / relitigating one
- Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively
- Acting alone / waiting too long
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, remember the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team itself: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and a direction everyone has agreed. Trust those, because they're how good work gets done together.
